tagline.text: A small Japanese dining lane in Makati, with torii gates and lanterns over izakaya and ramen shops

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of Chino Roces Avenue and Fernando Street, Makati (next to Makati Central Square)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (evenings recommended; the November–May dry season is easier for walking)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~2,500 (per person for a meal; varies a lot by menu, check locally)

children.text: Little Tokyo is a small Japanese dining lane at the corner of Chino Roces Avenue and Fernando Street in Makati, where the lanterns were first lit in 1999. Izakaya, yakiniku, ramen shops and Japanese grocers cluster between its torii gates, making it a good place for dinner and a drink.

Little Tokyo is a Japanese dining lane at the corner of Chino Roces Avenue and Fernando Street, a few blocks from Makati's central business district. OpenStreetMap marks it as a small commercial area at roughly 14.5537 N, 121.0142 E, and the Wikipedia entry for Chino Roces Avenue points to nearly the same spot. The avenue itself was formerly called Pasong Tamo and is described on Wikipedia as renamed in 1988 by a Makati resolution after the journalist Joaquin "Chino" Roces (who died that September). Wikipedia explains that the stretch from Rufino Street to Arnaiz Avenue is called Little Tokyo because of its many Japanese restaurants and shops.

In the narrow sense, Little Tokyo is a small compound with a Japanese-style bridge and torii gates inside the lane. It has two entrances, one on Chino Roces Avenue and one on Fernando Street, and the food outlet Primer says its lanterns were lit in 1999. It has since become a gathering place for Japanese expats and food lovers, and Japanese restaurants have spread into neighboring buildings such as Makati Central Square, Creekside and Beacon Tower. So what people call Little Tokyo today is closer to the compound plus a few surrounding blocks.

The atmosphere feels like a tiny version of a Tokyo back alley. Colorful signs and lanterns line the lane, many restaurants have outdoor seating enclosed by wooden partitions, and some are described as having small gardens, ponds or bonsai. Many people say it looks best in the evening when the lanterns are lit. It is not a sightseeing spot with many things to see; the focus is on eating and drinking. There is no admission fee and no set opening hours for the lane itself, only each restaurant's own hours.

Things do change. One restaurant (Hana), loved for takoyaki and Japanese dishes for 16 years since 2010, closed on March 24, 2026, citing rising costs, aging equipment and safety concerns after robberies targeting Japanese nationals. Others, like Oishinbo, which had operated since 2006, have also closed. On the other hand, long-running places such as Izakaya Kikufuji, open since 1995, as well as Sekitori, Seryna and Shinjuku ramen, were still listed as operating in a mid-2026 guide. Because the lineup changes often, please check on a map app and the restaurant's Facebook page before you go.

The entrance on the Chino Roces Avenue side has a torii gate and a Japanese-style bridge, which gives you the Japanese mood right away. There is also a torii gate on the Fernando Street side. The mood is best after dark, when the lanterns are lit.

An old izakaya operating since 1995, known for sashimi, sushi, chirashi-don and wagyu cube steak. It is described as serving separate lunch and dinner sessions, so it may be closed in the middle of the afternoon.

Sekitori is known for ebi tempura (shrimp tempura), donburi, udon and ramen, and its staff are described as wearing kimono. Seryna has sushi bar seating that suits solo diners and is also mentioned as a date-night spot.

Kagura serves okonomiyaki, yakisoba and tonpeiyaki, with counter seats where you can watch the cook. It used to take cash only, and 2023-2026 reviews say it now also takes GCash (with a P15 surcharge) and bank transfer but has no card terminal, so it is safer to bring cash.

There are meat restaurants such as Yakiniku A5 Toku, which serves A5 wagyu yakiniku, and Urameshi-Ya, where you grill your own beef, and nearby buildings continue with yakitori and izakaya. Wagyu courses are expensive, so check the price before ordering.

blocks.title: Ramen shops such as Menya Ippondo

children.text: There are ramen shops such as Menya Ippondo (formerly Ramen Shimada) and Shinjuku Home of Authentic Ramen. According to a July 2025 Primer listing, Ippondo is open from 3:30 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. on weekdays (from 11:30 a.m. on weekends; hours may change, so check), which makes it a candidate when you want a bowl of broth late at night.

Yamazaki is described as selling bento and ramen along with Japanese snacks and groceries, and Choto Stop is a small grocer selling soba and bento. Seikyo is also known as a Japanese grocery. They are good stops when you miss Korean or Japanese snacks.

Makati Central Square, the former Makati Cinema Square, is a 1980s building with phone accessory and secondhand record shops, a bowling alley, a shooting range and more. There is also said to be a Poblacion-style bar in the basement, so it is worth a look after dinner.

items.title: Dinner course
items.subtitle: Arrive when the lanterns light up, then eat and drink

children.text: Walk over slowly from Makati Greenbelt or the Legazpi side, or take a car, and arrive at Little Tokyo. A 2019 Primer guide says it is within about a 15-minute walk of Greenbelt or Legazpi Park, but because of the heat and walking conditions a taxi or Grab is more comfortable in the evening.

Take photos in front of the torii gate and Japanese-style bridge, and look over the restaurant signs in the lane, comparing menus and prices. If you are thinking of an izakaya or yakiniku, ask at this point whether there are seats.
Have dinner. Sharing sashimi or sushi, yakitori and okonomiyaki lets you try several dishes. Some places accept only cash, so bring cash.
After the meal, buy snacks and drinks at a nearby Japanese grocery or look around neighboring Makati Central Square. Late at night, decide on your transport in advance for safety.
Many sources say restaurants close for a break between lunch and dinner, so around 17:00 is the safest time to arrive.

items.title: Lunch course
items.subtitle: A light meal of bento and ramen

children.text: Eat a bento set, ramen or donburi at a restaurant serving lunch. Lunch sets usually come with rice, soup and salad.
Browse sauces, snacks and instant foods at a Japanese grocery. Check expiration dates and country-of-origin labels before buying.
After lunch, some restaurants go on break. This is a good time to move on to other sights in Makati.

items.title: Taxi or Grab from the airport or central Manila

children.text: The easiest way from Ninoy Aquino International Airport or central Manila is a taxi or Grab to Chino Roces Avenue in Makati. Setting your destination to Little Tokyo or Makati Central Square in a map app is accurate.
Makati has heavy traffic at rush hour, so travel time varies a lot by time of day. Check the fare and travel time in the app beforehand.
Chino Roces Avenue is a major road that meets EDSA, Gil Puyat Avenue and Kalayaan Avenue.

Chino Roces Avenue itself has no railway station. You can transfer to a taxi or jeepney from a nearby station such as MRT-3 Buendia, but it is best to confirm the exact route and transfers in a map app.

It is said to be about a 15-minute walk from Makati Greenbelt or Legazpi Park (2019 guide; the straight-line distance from Greenbelt's Wikipedia coordinates is about 0.9 km). Even so, keep the midday heat and sidewalk conditions in mind.
Parking inside the compound is said to be limited. You can use parking lots in nearby buildings such as Makati Central Square, Creekside and the Legazpi car park.

Little Tokyo mixes indoor and outdoor seating so you can visit year-round, but it is said to look best in the evening when the lanterns are lit. If you plan to sit outdoors, the drier months are more comfortable.
Many restaurants close between lunch and dinner, so check opening hours before you go.

Many hotels near Little Tokyo are close to central Makati. If you want to get around on foot, the hotels around Greenbelt and Legazpi Village give you more choices than the Chino Roces Avenue side, and late at night it is safer to travel by Grab.

The food falls into izakaya snacks, sushi, sashimi, okonomiyaki, takoyaki, yakiniku, ramen and donburi, and bento. Some of the shops listed in a 2023 article have already closed, so confirm whether a place is open. If Japanese food is your goal, one outlet also suggested alternatives such as Mitsukoshi in BGC, and in Makati ramen shops like The Underbelly at The Alley at Karrivin on Chino Roces Avenue Extension were awarded a Bib Gourmand in the first Michelin Guide Philippines (October 2025), so compare them to suit your situation.
Go in the evening, and check whether the restaurant closes between lunch and dinner.
Some restaurants accept only cash. Reviews say Kagura has no card terminal and charges extra for GCash. Bring plenty of cash.

A 2019 guide says there is a small smoking area inside the lane and that smoking is prohibited outside it, and some restaurants have their own smoking areas. Rules may have changed, so follow the on-site signs.
Before you go, check whether the restaurant is open and its hours on its Facebook page or Google Maps. Quite a few places have closed.
Check prices on the menu before ordering, and ask whether wagyu or sashimi is sold at market price.
Parking is difficult, so a Grab or taxi is more convenient.
The best photos are in front of the torii gate and Japanese-style bridge; inside restaurants, be careful not to include other guests.
When buying Japanese groceries, be sure to check the expiration date and labels.
Robberies targeting Japanese nationals were recently reported, and many shops have closed. At night, arrange your transport in advance and check the latest opening information.
A restaurant was reported to have closed in March 2026 citing safety concerns. Do not walk the lane alone late at night, and keep valuables close to your body.
Many restaurants in the 2019 and 2023 guides have closed. Do not rely on old blogs and reviews as they are.
There may be other businesses that merely share a name. The closed restaurant has stated that any business using its name is not related to it.
During heavy traffic hours, travel time increases a lot.
Opening hours and prices change often, so check the latest announcements.
Combine Little Tokyo with the museums, shopping and night views of the wider Makati area it belongs to.
